flags: minor: 'tested and revised' is slightly generous since the passage describes reasoning and objections more than tests, but it is clearly the best fit
R005-01.notes: Passage walks through pressure, friction and Faraday's surface-layer explanations and explains why views shifted. A contradicts paragraph 5; B is wrong because Faraday proposed the layer and modern measurements detected it; C is too narrow.

R005-02.notes: Paragraph 2 says pressure cannot explain why a stationary shoe slides just as readily. B is something pressure could explain on a mild day; C is about friction; D is a premise of the pressure account.

R005-03.notes: Paragraph 3: ice is slippery at the very first instant of a step, before heat builds up. A contradicts the cited experiments; B and D are unsupported.

flags: minor: the correct choice D is noticeably the longest, which is a length cue
R005-04.notes: 'Tidy, memorable' explains why the account sticks, and it is immediately followed by 'largely wrong.' B contradicts 'largely wrong'; C contradicts 'physicists who have checked the numbers.'

flags: minor: 'tidiness' (B) is a reasonable trap because it echoes 'tidy' in paragraph 1
R005-05.notes: 'The order of the story' means the sequence: the surface is slippery before anyone steps on it.

R005-06.notes: Faraday's account predicts slipperiness without heating, while friction needs motion and heat. A supports friction; C supports pressure; D is irrelevant and also scientifically dubious, since lower air pressure at altitude actually raises ice's melting point very slightly.

R005-07.notes: Surface molecules have fewer neighbors and are loosely bound, so interior molecules are held more firmly. A describes the surface molecules instead; B is wrong because Faraday proposed the layer and modern researchers measured it.

R005-08.notes: 'None of this means pressure and friction play no role' plus 'slippery before anyone steps on it.' A contradicts the paragraph; C and D are unsupported.

flags: minor: 'fifteen degrees below zero' gives no unit (C or F); the argument holds either way
R005-09.notes: Paragraph 2: pressure might matter on a mild afternoon, when the ice is already close to melting. B, C and D are the cases the passage says pressure cannot explain.

flags: minor: the correct choice D is the longest and most hedged, a common test-wise tell
R005-10.notes: 'Modern measurements have detected such a layer, though researchers still debate...' A and B are too negative; C contradicts both the open debate and paragraph 5.
